_how_to_edit: This file is the whole knowledge base of the Oman chatbot. Edit only the text between quotation marks.
Every question is one block between { and }. Keep the commas between blocks and between lines, and keep every quotation mark.
id = a short unique name. category = the group. keywords = words or phrases a visitor might type (lower case). answer = what the chatbot says.
volatile = true means the answer can change (visa, prices, opening times, dates). The chatbot then adds the 'please verify' note automatically.
contact = true means the chatbot also shows the phone / WhatsApp / email / contact-page options under the answer.
Answers: 3 to 5 sentences, neutral and friendly. Never write a fact you are not sure of.

faqs.answer: Entry rules depend on your nationality. Citizens of many countries can enter for a short stay without a visa, while others need to apply for an eVisa before travelling. Your passport must be valid and meet Oman's entry conditions.

Visitors who need a visa usually apply online through the official Royal Oman Police eVisa system before travelling. You will normally need a passport copy, a photo and payment of the fee. Processing times and fees are set by the authorities.

Short-stay entry is typically granted for around 14 days for visa-exempt nationalities, and tourist eVisas are commonly issued for up to 30 days. The exact length depends on your nationality and the visa type.

Travellers are generally advised to hold a passport valid for at least six months from the date of arrival, with blank pages for stamps. Airlines can refuse boarding if this is not met, so check before you fly.

Visa extensions are handled by the Royal Oman Police and are subject to their rules and fees. Staying beyond your permitted period can lead to fines, so arrange any extension before your visa expires.
Many visitors are advised to arrange an eVisa in advance rather than rely on getting one at the airport. Rules for arrival vary by nationality and can change.
Children generally need their own passport and, where a visa is required, their own visa. Requirements for minors can differ, so confirm the details on the official eVisa site.

Musandam is separated from the rest of Oman by UAE territory, so road journeys between them cross the UAE border and need valid travel documents. Rules for transiting the UAE and for entering Oman at the Musandam border depend on nationality and can change.
Arriving adult non-Muslim travellers may bring a limited amount of alcohol under customs rules. Allowances are set by Omani customs and can change, so please check before you travel.

Carry prescription medicines in their original packaging with a doctor's note or prescription. Some medicines that are legal elsewhere are controlled in Oman, so check the rules for your medication before travelling. Illegal drugs carry severe penalties.

Drones generally need official permission to bring in and to fly in Oman. Flying without approval can lead to confiscation or penalties, so it is best to check with the authorities before packing one.

Many visitors find October to April most comfortable, with warm days and pleasant evenings. Summer is very hot in most regions, but Salalah turns green during the khareef monsoon season. The best time depends on where you plan to go.
Muscat is most comfortable from roughly November to March, when days are warm and sunny. Summers are very hot and humid, so outdoor sightseeing is better done early or late in the day.

Salalah's khareef season, roughly late June to mid-September, brings mist, light rain and green hills, and is popular with regional visitors. The sea can be rough then, so swimming is often restricted. Outside khareef, Salalah is sunny and warm, especially in winter.
The mountains are cooler than the coast and are pleasant for hiking from autumn to spring. Winter nights can be cold at altitude, so bring warm layers. Summer days remain hot in the lower valleys.

Desert camping is most comfortable from roughly October to April, when days are warm and nights are cool. In summer, daytime temperatures in the desert are very high, so activities are usually limited to early morning and evening.
Musandam is generally best from autumn to spring, with pleasant sea trips and dhow cruises. Summers are very hot and humid on the coast.

Green turtles nest on the east coast, and guided turtle-watching visits at Ras Al Jinz take place at night. Nesting happens throughout much of the year with a peak in the warmer months, but sightings can never be guaranteed. Visits are guided and must be booked in advance.

Summer in much of Oman is very hot, so activities are best planned for early morning or evening. The Dhofar region around Salalah is the exception, with a cooler, misty khareef season. Hotels and some attractions can offer lower rates in the hot months.

Winters are mild on the coast, with sunny days and cooler evenings. In the mountains it can be cold, especially at night, so pack a warm layer. Rain is uncommon but can happen, mainly between December and March.

Oman has a hot, mostly dry climate. Coastal areas are humid in summer and temperatures can exceed 40 degrees Celsius, while the mountains stay noticeably cooler. Winter temperatures are comfortable in most places.

Rain is infrequent in most of Oman, but short heavy showers can occur, mainly in winter and spring. Dhofar has its own khareef drizzle in summer. After heavy rain, dry riverbeds called wadis can flood very quickly.
Humidity is highest on the coast in summer, which can make the heat feel more intense. Inland and mountain areas feel drier. Light clothing and plenty of water help.
The sun is strong all year, so sunscreen, sunglasses and a hat are recommended. Drink plenty of water, and plan outdoor activities for the cooler parts of the day.

Pack light, breathable clothing that covers shoulders and knees, plus sun protection and comfortable shoes. A light jacket is useful for cool mountain evenings or air-conditioned places. Swimwear is fine for beaches and hotel pools.
Oman's currency is the Omani rial (OMR), which is divided into 1,000 baisa. It is one of the higher-valued currencies in the world, so amounts often look small in rials.
Cards are widely accepted in hotels, restaurants and shops in cities. Cash is still useful in souqs, small towns and rural areas, so carry some rials.
ATMs are common in cities and towns and usually accept international cards. In remote areas they can be scarce, so withdraw cash before heading out of town.
You can exchange money at banks, licensed exchange offices and at the airport. The rial has long been tied to the US dollar, but rates and fees vary, so compare before exchanging.
Tipping is appreciated but not obligatory. Around 10 percent is a common guide in restaurants if no service charge has been added, and small amounts for porters or drivers are welcome.
Polite bargaining is normal in traditional souqs, especially for souvenirs and silver. In shops with fixed prices and in malls, prices are not negotiated.
Oman applies value-added tax on many goods and services, and hotels may add service and municipality charges. Rates and rules can change, so check what is included in a price.

Oman can be a mid-range to higher-cost destination compared with some of its neighbours, particularly for hotels and desert camps. Costs vary a lot by season and travel style. For a quote for your trip, our team can help.

Most visitors travel by rental car, private driver or organised tour, as distances are large and public transport is limited outside Muscat. Taxis and ride-hailing apps operate in cities, and domestic flights connect Muscat with Salalah and Khasab.

Car rental is easy in Muscat and other main cities, and roads are generally good. You will usually need a valid driving licence, a credit card for the deposit and to meet the age requirement of the rental company. Check insurance and whether your plans need a 4x4.
Many visitors can drive with their home licence, and an International Driving Permit is often recommended. Rules depend on your nationality and the rental company, so check in advance.
Traffic in Oman drives on the right-hand side of the road. Speed cameras are common, and speed limits are enforced, so keep to the signed limits.

A normal car is fine for main roads, cities and most major sights. A 4x4 is needed for dune driving, some wadis and mountain tracks, and driving off-road without experience is not advised. Many visitors use a guide for these areas.
Taxis are available in Muscat and other cities and at the airport. Agree the fare before starting or ask for the meter, and carry small notes for payment.
Ride-hailing apps operate in Muscat and some other cities, which is a convenient way to get taxis with set fares. Availability can vary by area, so check which app works where you are.

Mwasalat, the national transport company, runs city and intercity buses between Muscat and several destinations. Services and timetables can change, and buses are less flexible than a car or tour for sightseeing.
There are domestic flights from Muscat to Salalah and to Khasab in Musandam. Flight times are short compared with the long drive to Salalah, but schedules vary by season.

Muscat to Nizwa is about 165 km, roughly one and a half to two hours by road. Muscat to the Wahiba Sands is roughly two and a half to three hours. Muscat to Salalah is around 1,000 km, so most visitors fly.
Fuel stations are frequent on main roads, but can be far apart in remote areas, so fill up before long desert or mountain drives. Fuel prices are set by the authorities and can change.
Seat belts are required, mobile phone use while driving is not allowed and speed cameras are widespread. There is zero tolerance for drink-driving. Fines are enforced, so follow signs and limits.
Muscat International Airport is the main gateway, with taxis, ride-hailing and car-rental desks available. Salalah and Khasab also have airports for domestic and some regional flights.

Oman is a conservative country, and modest dress is appreciated. Shoulders and knees should generally be covered in public, loose, light clothing works well in the heat. Swimwear is fine at beaches and hotel pools.
Women are advised to cover shoulders and knees, and loose-fitting clothes are most comfortable. A headscarf is not required in general but is needed when entering mosques.
Men should avoid sleeveless tops and are advised to wear trousers or knee-length shorts in towns and cities. Long trousers are required when visiting mosques.

Visitors to a mosque should be fully covered, with long sleeves and long trousers or skirts, and women should cover their hair. Shoes are removed at the entrance. The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque in Muscat admits non-Muslim visitors at set hours, which can change.
Swimwear is fine at resort beaches and hotel pools. On public beaches, modest swimwear and cover-ups when leaving the water are advised. Nudity and topless sunbathing are not permitted.

A friendly 'As-salamu alaykum' is a welcome greeting, and visitors are often greeted warmly in return. When shaking hands, it is polite to wait for the other person to offer, especially across genders.
Always ask permission before photographing people, especially women. Avoid photographing military sites, government buildings and airports, as well as other restricted areas.
Public displays of affection are discouraged in Oman, so it is best to keep these to a minimum. Hand-holding for married couples is generally acceptable.
Alcohol is available in licensed hotels and some restaurants, but not sold in general shops, and drinking in public places is not allowed. There is zero tolerance for drink-driving.

It is polite to use your right hand for eating, greeting and passing items. Accepting offered coffee and dates is a gesture of hospitality, and you can shake the cup lightly to show you have had enough.
If you are invited into a home, remove your shoes at the door and accept refreshments graciously. A small gift such as sweets is welcome.
Arabic is the official language, and English is widely spoken in hotels, restaurants and tourist services. Learning a few Arabic words such as 'shukran' (thank you) is appreciated.

Traditional Omani dishes include shuwa (slow-cooked marinated meat), majboos (spiced rice with meat or fish), mashuai (grilled kingfish with lemon rice) and harees (wheat and meat porridge). Dates, halwa and cardamom-spiced kahwa coffee are served as hospitality.
Shuwa is marinated meat wrapped in leaves and slow-cooked in an underground oven, often for a day or more. It is traditionally prepared for festive occasions such as Eid.
Kahwa is Omani coffee flavoured with cardamom and sometimes saffron, usually served with dates as a sign of hospitality. Omani halwa is a sweet, sticky dessert that is a popular gift.
Food in Oman is generally halal, and pork is not widely available outside some hotels and specialist shops.

Vegetarian options are easy to find, especially in cities, with many Indian, Lebanese and international restaurants. For vegan, allergy or gluten-free needs, it helps to tell restaurants in advance. Camps and rural areas have fewer choices.
Tap water is treated in cities, but most visitors prefer bottled water, which is cheap and widely available. Drink plenty of water in the heat.
Fresh fish and seafood are popular along the coast, and fish markets such as Mutrah in Muscat are worth a visit. Restaurants serve grilled fish with rice and local spices.
Oman is generally regarded as welcoming and has low levels of everyday crime. As anywhere, take normal precautions with valuables and follow local guidance, especially around heat, wadis and the sea.
Many women travel in Oman and report being treated respectfully, while dressing modestly is recommended. Normal precautions apply, such as using licensed taxis and sharing your plans.
The emergency number in Oman for police, ambulance and fire is 9999. Keep your embassy's details and your travel insurance information to hand.
Dry riverbeds called wadis can flood suddenly after rain, even if the rain falls far away. Never cross a flowing wadi, avoid camping in a wadi bed and check weather warnings before you go.
Heat can be dangerous, so drink plenty of water, wear a hat and avoid strenuous activity in the middle of the day. Seek shade and medical help if you feel dizzy or unwell.
Sea conditions can change quickly and some beaches have strong currents, especially in Dhofar during khareef. Swim only where it is safe, follow local warnings and flags and avoid swimming alone.
Travel insurance covering medical care and evacuation is strongly recommended. Private healthcare is good in main cities but can be expensive without cover.
Vaccination requirements depend on your nationality and where you have travelled from. Check current guidance with your doctor or national health authority before travelling.
Pharmacies and hospitals are found in cities and towns, and private clinics in Muscat offer good care. Remote areas have fewer facilities, so carry basic medication and a first-aid kit.
Snakes and scorpions exist in desert and rocky areas, but encounters are rare. Wear closed shoes outdoors and shake out shoes and bedding when camping. Mosquito repellent is useful in some areas.

Local SIM cards and tourist data packages are available from the airport and shops, usually requiring your passport. Wi-Fi is widely available in hotels and cafes, and coverage can be weak in remote desert and mountain areas.
Oman uses 240V electricity with UK-style three-pin (Type G) sockets. Bring an adapter if your devices use a different plug.
Oman uses Gulf Standard Time, UTC+4, all year round. There is no daylight saving time.

The weekend in Oman is Friday and Saturday. Many shops close for a break in the afternoon and reopen in the evening, and some places have limited hours on Fridays. Opening hours vary, so check before you go.
The call to prayer is heard five times a day. Some shops may pause briefly at prayer times, and visitors are asked to be quiet and respectful near mosques.
Many visitors spend around five to seven days to see Muscat, the mountains and the desert, and a little longer if adding Salalah or Musandam. The right length depends on your interests and pace.
Camping is popular in Oman, both at organised desert camps and in wild locations. Check local rules and weather conditions, avoid wadi beds because of flood risk, and leave no trace.

Muscat's highlights include the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque, Mutrah Souq and Corniche, the Royal Opera House, Al Alam Palace and the National Museum. The city also has beaches, wadis and mountain drives nearby.
The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque welcomes non-Muslim visitors at set morning hours, and a strict dress code applies. Opening times and visitor rules can change, so please verify before you go.
Mutrah Souq is one of Oman's oldest markets, known for frankincense, silver, textiles and souvenirs. It is lively in the evening, and polite bargaining is normal.
The Royal Opera House Muscat hosts concerts and performances and offers daytime tours. Programmes and visiting hours vary, so check in advance.
Muscat has several beaches, including Qurum and others along the coast, as well as resort beaches. Conditions vary by season, so follow local flags and advice.
Two to three days is usually enough to see Muscat's main sights at an easy pace. Add day trips to nearby wadis, the coast or mountain villages if you have more time.
Nizwa is known for its large round fort, traditional souq and its role as a historic capital of Oman. It makes a good base for visiting Jebel Akhdar, Bahla and nearby villages.
Nizwa's traditional Friday morning livestock market is a popular cultural sight. It tends to run in the early morning, and times can change, so please verify before you plan around it.
Nizwa Fort is one of Oman's most visited landmarks, with a tower you can climb. Opening hours and entry fees can change, so please check before visiting.
Around Nizwa you can visit Bahla Fort, Jabrin Castle, the old mud-brick town of Al Hamra and the mountain village of Misfat Al Abriyyin. They are easy to combine into a day trip.

Jebel Akhdar is a high plateau known for terraced gardens, cool air and village walks. Jebel Shams, nearby, has Oman's highest peak and dramatic canyon views. Both are cooler than the coast and some roads require a 4x4.
The Wahiba Sands, also called Sharqiya Sands, are a large area of rolling orange dunes in eastern Oman. Visitors enjoy dune driving, sunset views, camel rides and overnight stays at desert camps.

Desert camps range from simple tents to more comfortable camps with private facilities. They are usually reached by 4x4, with a guide or driver. Standards and prices vary, so ask for details when planning.
Driving on the dunes needs a suitable 4x4 and experience, so most visitors go with a local driver or guide. Lowering tyre pressure and local knowledge make a big difference to safety.
Many visitors spend one night in the desert, arriving in the afternoon for sunset and staying for sunrise. It is typically combined with Wadi Bani Khalid or the east coast.

Wadi Bani Khalid is a green wadi with natural pools close to the Wahiba Sands, and Wadi Shab is a popular canyon walk and swim on the coast. Modest swimwear is advised, and conditions can change after rain.
Salalah, in Dhofar, is known for its coast, frankincense trees and the green khareef season. Highlights include Al Baleed Archaeological Park, Mughsail blowholes, Wadi Darbat and the old souqs.

Frankincense is a resin from trees that grow in Dhofar and has been traded from the region for thousands of years. Sites such as Al Baleed in Salalah are part of the UNESCO-listed Land of Frankincense.
Salalah is about 1,000 km from Muscat, so most visitors fly, with the flight taking under two hours. Driving is possible but long and passes through remote desert.
During khareef, the hills around Salalah turn green and temperatures are mild, which attracts many visitors from across the region. Accommodation can be busy and more expensive then, so book early.
Salalah has attractive beaches, but strong currents and rough seas during khareef make swimming unsafe at that time. The Mughsail blowholes are a popular viewpoint in summer.
Musandam is a rugged peninsula known for dramatic fjord-like inlets, dhow cruises and mountain scenery. Khasab is the main base, with boat trips, dolphin watching and snorkelling.
Half-day and full-day dhow cruises from Khasab visit the fjords and offer chances to see dolphins and go snorkelling. Sea conditions and operators' schedules vary.
You can reach Musandam by a domestic flight to Khasab or by road through the UAE, which involves a border crossing. Check that your travel documents meet the requirements for both routes.
Many visitors spend one to two nights in Khasab to enjoy a dhow cruise and a mountain drive. It can be visited as a short add-on or as a day trip from the UAE.
Jebel Harim is Musandam's high mountain with sweeping views. The road up is steep and best done in a suitable vehicle or with a guide.
The coastal town of Sur is known for its traditional dhow-building yard and lighthouses. Nearby Ras Al Hadd and Ras Al Jinz are famous for turtle nesting on the beaches.

Oman's UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Bahla Fort, the archaeological sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn, the Land of Frankincense and the Aflaj irrigation systems. The list can change, so check UNESCO for the current sites.
Travel Store Oman helps travellers plan trips in Oman. Our team is based in Muscat and can answer questions about tours and trip planning.
The easiest way to start is to send us your travel dates, group size and interests, and our team will advise on the options. We can help with tours, transfers and itinerary ideas.
Both private and group options are commonly available for Oman tours. Availability depends on the dates and the tour, so please get in touch to confirm what is offered.
We can help shape trips around your dates and interests, from short city stays to longer journeys across the country. Please contact our team with your ideas and they will be happy to assist.
Prices depend on the season, group size, accommodation and activities, so I can't give an accurate figure here. Our team will gladly prepare a quote for you.
Cancellation and change terms depend on the booking and the supplier. Please contact our team to discuss your booking.
What is included varies by tour, so I can't confirm details here. Our team can tell you exactly what each trip covers.

Oman is a family-friendly destination, with beaches, forts and easy wadi walks suited to children. Long drives and the summer heat are worth planning around for younger travellers. Our team can suggest suitable trips.
Accessibility varies by site and activity, as many forts and wadis have steps or uneven ground. Our team can advise on what suits your needs.

Ramadan is the Islamic holy month of fasting from dawn to sunset. Travel is possible, but visitors are asked not to eat, drink or smoke in public during the day, and some cafes and restaurants adjust their hours. Evenings are lively with iftar meals.

Ramadan moves earlier by roughly ten to eleven days each year because it follows the Islamic lunar calendar. The exact start is announced locally based on moon sighting, so please check close to the time.
Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan and Eid al-Adha follows the pilgrimage season. Many businesses close for several days and the dates are set by moon sighting, so check before planning.
Oman's National Day is celebrated on 18 November. Public holidays include Renaissance Day and the Islamic holidays, with some dates set by moon sighting and subject to announcement.
On public holidays and during Ramadan, opening hours at shops, offices and some attractions may be reduced. It is wise to confirm hours for anywhere you want to visit.
